children: Australia's financial system regulator said on Friday it contacted banks and pension funds following the collapse of Bathla Group, adding their exposure to the debt-laden home builder was limited.

Bathla, which operates in Sydney's western suburbs and is one of the country's biggest affordable housing developers, went into administration last month owing more than A$3 billion ($2.15 billion) to dozens of private lenders.

The collapse highlighted the risks of Australia's rapidly growing private credit sector, but also raised concerns about potential spillover into the broader financial system through unpaid debts Bathla owed to subcontractors, suppliers and vendors.
The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) said it had engaged with the entities it regulated about Bathla.

The banking industry had "negligible" exposure to the firm, but "monitoring the interplay between regulated entities and private credit supports the safety and soundness of our banks and the financial system", an APRA spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
While APRA said pension fund trustees should maintain robust investment governance and ensure they applied appropriate valuations, the funds it regulated also had little direct exposure to Bathla.
"Trustees' due diligence and investment governance, including valuation, of unlisted and illiquid investments has been a point of ongoing focus for APRA," the regulator said.
Administrators for Bathla on Monday secured two weeks of funding to allow some of the beleaguered home builder's operations to continue.
They said "significant work" remained to find a long-term rescue deal, raising the prospect of liquidation that could put thousands of homes under construction at risk.
